loops.operand_stats: uECC_WORD_SIZE=8 on the x86_64 profiling host (4 x 64-bit limbs per 256-bit field element); on RV32 it builds the WORD_SIZE==4 variant (8 x 32-bit limbs, curve-specific.inc:883). Input is a 512-bit product (8 limbs) and the output is a 256-bit residue mod p256. Work is 8 limb-wise add/sub chains of 4 limbs (s1..s4 added, d1..d4 subtracted, plus two doubling adds) with operands built by 32-bit-granularity shift/OR/mask of product[4..7]. The serial recurrence is carry/borrow propagation across limbs, done in software as compare-and-select (sum<left / diff>left) because base RV has no carry flag. Final correction is a data-dependent loop of conditional add/sub of p, usually 0-2 iterations. All memory access is sequential and unit-stride over small stack arrays. Called once per modular multiply (530,967 calls), so it is on every field-mult path.

Product-scanning (Comba) schoolbook multiply of two 256-bit operands. On the 64-bit host that is num_words=4, giving 16 muladd per call; on RV32 it is num_words=8, giving 64 muladd per call. uECC_SQUARE_FUNC=0, so squarings also come through here (3,694,592 calls). Each muladd is one full WxW->2W unsigned multiply (needs MUL + MULHU on RISC-V) accumulated into a 3-word accumulator (r0,r1,r2), with carry detection by compare. The loop-carried recurrence is the triple-word accumulator, a natural fit for a fused multiply-accumulate-with-carry instruction. Memory access: left[i] ascending and right[k-i] descending, both unit-stride and read-only; one store per output column. Operands are full-width, uniformly random field elements.

Modular subtraction over 4x64-bit limbs (8x32 on RV32). The borrow-propagation recurrence runs across limbs, and a conditional add of p follows when the subtraction borrows (about 50% for random operands). It uses the same add/sub-with-carry primitive as the mmod_fast reduction. Calls are frequent but short (3,939,328 calls, around 140 cycles each), coming from the XYcZ_add/XYcZ_addC/double_jacobian point formulas. Memory access is sequential and unit-stride.
